opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm more bullish than people might expect, given that most of my work is on the formal-verification side of things.

Self-other overlap appeals to me because it isn't just "train the model to say nice things." The idea is to shape internal representations so that when the model processes "what's good for me" and "what's good for others," those computations share structure. That intervenes on something closer to the mechanism of deception and self-interest than behavioral fine-tuning does. And there's a nice intuition from neuroscience and evolution: empathy in humans plausibly works partly through this kind of overlap. We model others with the same machinery we use to model ourselves, and that makes it harder to coldly instrumentalize them.

Early results suggest you can reduce deceptive behavior in toy settings without destroying capabilities, which is the key tradeoff to watch. If you collapse self and other entirely, you get a model that can't reason about other agents' beliefs, which is useless and possibly dangerous. So it's about finding the right amount of overlap.

But I'd put it in a specific place in the overall portfolio. I don't think any technique that operates on learned representations in a giant neural network gives us strong guarantees on its own. You're relying on the overlap generalizing to situations you didn't train on, and on the model not routing around it as capabilities scale. A sufficiently capable system under optimization pressure could develop new internal pathways that don't share the overlap structure. So it's a probabilistic improvement in the prior over AI dispositions, not a proof.

Where I get excited is the combination. In the Safeguarded AI framing, we want AI systems to produce artifacts like world models, specifications, and controllers that can be checked independently, so we don't have to fully trust the AI. But you still have to trust the AI somewhat during that process. You want it to be cooperative and to not sabotage the work subtly. That's exactly where dispositional techniques like self-other overlap earn their keep. They make the "mostly cooperative" assumption more realistic, and verification catches what slips through.

So: bullish as a layer of defense in depth, and as one of the more principled ideas in the mechanistic alignment space. Not bullish as a standalone solution. I'd love to see it stress-tested on frontier-scale models, with adversarial evaluations specifically trying to find where the overlap breaks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think I'd separate two things there, because "mechanistic" is doing a lot of work in that question. There's mechanistic interpretability as a scientific program, which I'm actually fairly positive on, and then there's this newer family of what I'd call mechanistic interventions, where you reach into the network and try to shape the representations directly, and self-other overlap is probably the cleanest example of that.

On self-other overlap specifically, I find the core idea genuinely appealing. The intuition is that a lot of what we're worried about, deception, manipulation, treating the human as an adversary to be modeled and outmaneuvered, requires the model to maintain a sharp internal distinction between "my goals, my knowledge" and "their goals, their knowledge." If you can regularize the model so that its representation of itself and its representation of the other party are closer together, you might get something like honesty or cooperation falling out of the geometry rather than having to specify it. That's elegant. It also has this nice property that it's not a behavioral patch. You're not just training away the bad outputs you happened to catch. And the early results people have shown, on relatively small models, are not nothing.

But here's where my bullishness runs out. The thing I keep coming back to is: what's the argument that it holds? Not "it worked on these benchmarks," but what's the structural reason to believe that a model which has been nudged toward self-other overlap, and then scaled up, and then put through more optimization pressure, retains that property in exactly the situations where it matters? Those are precisely the situations we can't test in advance. And with any technique that operates on the representations without an actual understanding of what those representations compute, you're essentially hoping the correlation you found at small scale is causal and robust, and I don't think we have a theory that licenses that hope yet.

There's also a more subtle failure mode. If you apply a regularizer that penalizes the model for distinguishing self from other, a sufficiently capable system could satisfy that regularizer superficially, make the activations look overlapped under whatever probe you're using, while still computing the distinction somewhere you're not measuring. That's not a hypothetical weirdness, that's just what optimization does to proxies. So the technique's success depends heavily on how good your measurement of "overlap" is, which brings you right back to the interpretability problem it was supposed to help you route around.

So my honest position is something like: cautiously interested as a research direction, not something I'd want anyone to lean on as a safety case. And this is really my broader view. I think the techniques that modify the model's internals are valuable mostly insofar as they feed into a story we could actually verify, with some kind of guarantee attached. If self-other overlap turned out to give you a property you could state precisely and then check, that would be exciting. If it's "we did this training trick and the deception metrics went down," then it's one more empirical finding in a field that has a lot of empirical findings and not many guarantees. I'd rather we spend our effort making the guarantee part possible than keep accumulating promising-looking heuristics.

astra-6.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic. I think mechanistic approaches are valuable because they try to get underneath the behavior and ask what computation the system is actually doing. But there’s a substantial gap between finding a mechanism that seems to promote cooperation and establishing that it will reliably do so as the system becomes more capable.

With something like self-other overlap, the interesting question is what exactly is overlapping. Sharing representations of yourself and another agent doesn’t, by itself, imply that you care about that agent’s welfare. It might help you predict them. So I’d want to understand the causal connection to the system’s decisions, and then ask whether that connection survives further training and unfamiliar situations.

I’m bullish on investigating these ideas. I’m more cautious about treating any one of them as a sufficient basis for confidence in alignment. The direction I find most compelling is connecting mechanistic understanding to explicit properties we can test and, where possible, verify.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic. I think self-other overlap is an interesting hypothesis: if a model uses some of the same machinery to represent itself and other agents, perhaps you can use that to encourage it to take their interests seriously. But there’s a substantial gap between finding overlapping representations and establishing that the system will behave benevolently, particularly as it becomes more capable.

What I’d want to understand is the causal mechanism. Does intervening on that overlap reliably change behavior? Does the effect survive further training, distribution shift, and situations where the system has an incentive to deceive us? And does it generalize beyond the particular agents or scenarios used during training?

So I’m bullish on investigating these techniques and using them as components of a broader alignment strategy. I’m much less comfortable treating any one of them as a sufficient safety argument. My own emphasis is on getting to explicit specifications and checkable guarantees, so we can distinguish a promising empirical effect from something we can actually rely on.
